title: The Small Postcard
premise: Rosalind Thornbury has built a career on erasing herself—ghostwriting the glittering memoirs of her rival, socialite Camille Ashford, while nursing a decade-old heartbreak she blames on her own cowardice. When her mother's seventieth-birthday reunion threatens to expose every lie Rosalind has told about her life, she hires Julian Reeve, a charming stranger from a bookshop, to pose as her boyfriend for one weekend. But Julian turns out to be Camille's estranged brother and the memoir's unnamed source, and by dessert their fake romance feels dangerously real. As deadline and family secrets collide, Rosalind must choose between the invisible safety of her old identity and a visible, forgivable self—and in the end she claims her own name on the page, confesses everything to both families, and chooses Julian not as an escape but as an equal.
about_author: Xanthe Underhill is the pen name of a former publishing insider who spent years writing other people's love stories before daring to claim one of her own. She lives by the sea with a typewriter, a dog named Margot, and a firm belief that second drafts, like second chances, are where the truth gets in.

chapters.title: Past Tense
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Late at night in her cramped flat, Rosalind polishes Chapter Twelve of Camille Ashford's memoir, deleting a passage that cuts too close to her own buried romance with a man called J. Her editor calls: the manuscript is due in six weeks. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as discipline; we see a woman fluent in everyone's voice but her own.

chapters.title: The Invitation
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A gilt-edged summons arrives for her mother's seventieth reunion at Thornbury Hall, complete with a guest list demanding 'plus ones.' Her sister Imogen texts a warning: Aunt Prudence will interrogate. Panicked, Rosalind invents a boyfriend on the spot. Emotional beat: comic dread masking real shame about the smallness of the life she's built.

chapters.title: The Man in the Bookshop
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian Reeve, restocking poetry in his uncle's Charing Cross bookshop, is ambushed by a flustered woman offering him money to be her boyfriend for a weekend. Amused, broke, and intrigued, he negotiates terms over tea. Emotional beat: playful spark; Julian recognizes something wounded beneath Rosalind's brisk efficiency and says yes for reasons he doesn't examine.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Over one chaotic afternoon, Rosalind and Julian build their fake history—how they met, first kiss, favorite songs—while accidentally revealing true details neither meant to share. A practice kiss in the kitchen goes on too long. Emotional beat: intimacy through invention; the fiction they're constructing keeps slipping into confession.

chapters.title: Thornbury Hall
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Arrival at the reunion: her mother's brittle elegance, Imogen's sharp protectiveness, Aunt Prudence circling like a customs officer. Julian performs flawlessly, charming even the gardener, but Rosalind spots a familiar surname on the seating chart—Reeve—and her stomach drops. Emotional beat: dread braided with warmth; the performance starts working too well.

chapters.title: By Dessert
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. During dinner, Julian realizes Rosalind is the ghostwriter behind his sister Camille's memoir—the project that dragged their family secrets into print and estranged them. He says nothing. Later, alone on the terrace, their staged banter becomes a real conversation about failure and forgiveness, ending almost in a kiss. Emotional beat: desire tangled with betrayal; dessert tastes like guilt.

chapters.title: What Camille Knew
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Confronted by a chapter draft Camille slipped into her bag, Rosalind learns the memoir deliberately exposed the Reeve family to bury a scandal of its own—and that her words were weaponized. She also learns Julian knew who she was before the bookshop. Emotional beat: fury and vertigo; the person she trusted most may have been running his own con.

chapters.title: The Mirror Room
chapters.summary: Imogen's POV. Imogen finds Rosalind shattered in the hall's mirrored drawing room and forces the truth out: ten years ago Rosalind abandoned a man named Jonah—not because he failed her, but because she couldn't bear being seen loving anyone more than her work. Imogen delivers the novel's thesis: invisibility was never survival, only slow disappearance. Emotional beat: catharsis; forgiveness begins inward.

chapters.title: Deadline
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The final manuscript is due; Camille demands Rosalind sign away authorship forever or lose everything. Julian offers to expose Camille if Rosalind will just walk away with him quietly. Instead, Rosalind does the unthinkable: she puts her own name on the title page, sends the memoir to a rival publisher with her exposé attached, and tells Julian the truth about Jonah—and about wanting him, visibly, on purpose. Emotional beat: climax; courage costs everything and buys her back.

chapters.title: The Small Postcard
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, epilogue. Months later, Rosalind's debut novel under her own name sits in the bookshop window where they met. A small postcard arrives from Julian—now reconciled with Camille—containing a single line: 'Dinner? No rehearsal this time.' She writes back yes. Emotional beat: resolution; love kept no longer in past tense, identity claimed, the mirror finally friendly.
